chapters.name: Chapter 1: Threats and how attacks work

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What cybersecurity protects
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain the three goals of security using the CIA triad.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short description of an attack, you will explain the three goals of security (confidentiality, integrity and availability) and identify which one the attack breaks, getting at least 4 of 5 examples right.
Security people often use three words, called the CIA triad. Confidentiality: only the right people can see the information, like your grades or medical records. Integrity: the information is correct and has not been changed by someone who should not change it, like a bank balance. Availability: the information and systems work when you need them, like a website that stays up.
Every attack hurts at least one of the three. Someone reading your messages breaks confidentiality. Someone changing a payment amount breaks integrity. Ransomware that locks a hospital's computers breaks availability.
The people who attack are called threat actors. They range from scammers looking for quick money to organized criminal groups. Most attacks on everyday people are not personal; attackers go after whoever is easiest.
Words to know:
- Cybersecurity: protecting computers, phones, accounts and information from attack.
- CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three goals of security.
- Threat actor: a person or group that attacks computers or accounts.
Try it now: Think of one app you use, such as a school portal, a bank app or a work schedule app. Write one example of what confidentiality, integrity and availability mean for it.
You can now explain the CIA triad and say which goal an attack breaks.

check.q: In the CIA triad, what does integrity mean?
options: The system is always fast
Only the right people can see the information
The information is free to everyone
The information is correct and has not been changed by someone who should not change it
check.why: Integrity means the information is correct and not changed without permission.

check.q: Someone reads a classmate's private messages without permission. Which goal would you say is broken?
options: Availability
Confidentiality
Integrity
None of the three
check.why: Confidentiality means only the right people can see the information.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Common attacks: malware, ransomware and account takeover
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the most common attacks and how each one usually gets in.
This lesson builds toward: Given examples of malware, ransomware, account takeover and social engineering, you will name each attack and describe how it usually gets in, with each attack named correctly and one common way in for each.
Malware is harmful software. It often arrives in an email attachment, a fake app, a pirated game or a fake "update" pop-up. Ransomware is malware that locks your files and demands payment to unlock them.
Account takeover happens when someone gets into your account. The most common ways are a stolen or guessed password, a password reused from another site that was breached, or tricking you into sharing a one-time code.
Social engineering means tricking a person instead of breaking the technology. A caller pretending to be IT support, a fake delivery text or a message from a "friend" asking for a code are all social engineering. People are often the easiest way in, which is why your habits matter.
Words to know:
- Malware: harmful software that can spy, steal or damage.
- Ransomware: malware that locks files and demands payment.
- Data breach: when a company's stored information, like passwords, is stolen.
- Social engineering: tricking a person into giving access or information.
Try it now: For each attack (malware, ransomware, account takeover, social engineering), write one real-life way it could reach you or your family, and one habit that would stop it.
You can now name the common attacks and how they usually get in.

check.q: Which of these is a common way malware gets onto a device?
options: A pirated game or a fake "update" pop-up
Turning on automatic updates
Using a password manager
Restarting your phone
check.why: Malware often arrives in attachments, fake apps, pirated games and fake update pop-ups.

check.q: A "friend" messages you asking for the code your phone just received. What would you do?
options: Send the code because it is a friend
Send half the code
Do not share the code; this is likely social engineering
Post the code on social media to check
check.why: Tricking you into sharing a one-time code is a common way accounts are taken over.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Spotting and reporting phishing
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick out a phishing message and report it the right way.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real or sample email or text, you will identify the phishing signs it shows and report it the right way, listing at least two signs and choosing a correct place to report it.
Phishing is a fake email, text or message that tries to get you to click a link, open a file or share information. The FTC lists common tricks: claiming suspicious activity on your account, a problem with your payment, asking you to confirm personal information, an invoice you do not recognize, a link to pay, a government refund, or a coupon for free stuff.
Check the sender's real address, not just the name. Hover over links on a computer (or press and hold on a phone) to see where they really go. Look for urgency: "act now or your account will close."
If you do not know the sender, report it and delete it. If you do have an account with that company, contact it using a website or phone number you already know is real, not the one in the message. The FTC says to forward phishing emails to reportphishing@apwg.org, forward phishing texts to SPAM (7726), and report to ReportFraud.ftc.gov. At school or work, use the "Report phishing" button or tell IT.
Step by step:
- Check the sender's real address.
- Hover over or long-press the link to see where it goes.
- Look for urgency, threats or prizes.
- Do not click, reply or open attachments.
- Contact the company using a number or site you already know.
- Report: email to reportphishing@apwg.org, texts to 7726, and ReportFraud.ftc.gov; at school or work tell IT.
Words to know:
- Phishing: a fake message that tries to trick you into clicking, opening a file or sharing information.
- Smishing: phishing by text message.
- Spoofing: faking a sender's name, number or address so a message looks real.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to recognize and avoid phishing scams
- FTC: ReportFraud
Try it now: Open your spam or junk folder (or your texts) and find one suspicious message. Without clicking anything, list every phishing sign you see, then report or delete it.
You can now spot a phishing message, avoid its traps and report it the right way.

check.q: On a phone, how can you see where a link really goes before you open it?
options: Tap it quickly twice
Press and hold the link
Reply to the sender
Turn the phone off and on
check.why: Pressing and holding shows the real address without opening it.

check.q: A text says your delivery is on hold and you must pay a small fee by link. You have no package coming. What would you do?
options: Pay the fee to be safe
Reply asking which package it is
Click the link to see what it says
Forward it to SPAM (7726), report it and delete it
check.why: The FTC says to forward phishing texts to SPAM (7726) and report them.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Strong passwords and a password manager
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a strong, unique password and save it in a password manager.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free password manager, you will create a strong, unique password for one important account and save it in the password manager, with a password of at least 16 characters that is not used on any other account.
CISA says a strong password is long (at least 16 characters), random, and unique (different for every account). A passphrase of four to seven unrelated words, like CISA's example "HorsePurpleHatRun", is long and easy to remember.
Nobody can remember a different strong password for every account, so use a password manager. It creates and stores passwords for you; you remember just one strong main password. CISA notes that some are free, including ones built into web browsers and phones.
Never share passwords, never type them into an AI tool, and change a password right away if a company tells you it was in a data breach.
Step by step:
- Open a password manager: the one built into your browser or phone, or a trusted app.
- Choose your most important account, usually email.
- Use the manager to create a long, random password, or make a 4 to 7 word passphrase.
- Save it in the manager.
- Change the password on the account and test signing in.
Words to know:
- Password manager: an app that creates and stores your passwords safely.
- Passphrase: a password made of several unrelated words.
- Unique password: a password used for only one account.
Official sources:
- CISA Secure Our World: Use strong passwords
Try it now: Open the password manager on your phone or browser. Use it to create and save a new strong password for one account you care about.
You can now create a strong, unique password and keep it in a password manager.

check.q: What does "unique" mean for a password?
options: It has your name in it
It is short and easy to type
It is different for every account
It is the same as your phone PIN
check.why: A unique password is used for one account only, so one breach does not open the others.

check.q: A company emails to say your password was in a data breach. What would you do?
options: Change that password right away
Wait to see if anything happens
Use the same password on a new account
Share the password with a friend to check it
check.why: Change a password right away when a company says it was in a breach.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Multifactor authentication and updates
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn on multifactor authentication and update a device.
This lesson builds toward: On one important account and your own device, you will turn on multifactor authentication and check that the device and apps are up to date, with MFA working on the account and automatic updates turned on.
Multifactor authentication (MFA) asks for a second proof after your password, such as a code from an authenticator app, a prompt on your phone, a security key, or a passkey. Even if someone steals your password, they cannot get in without the second factor. Turn it on for email, banking, school and social media first. CISA says any MFA is better than none, and the strongest kind is phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO, used by passkeys and security keys), which is harder to trick than a text code.
Never share an MFA code. If you get a code or login prompt you did not ask for, someone may have your password: deny it and change your password.
Updates fix security holes attackers already know about. Turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer, browser and apps, and restart when asked. CISA lists updating software as one of its four core steps, along with avoiding phishing, strong passwords and MFA.
Step by step:
- Open your email account's security settings.
- Find two-step verification, two-factor or multifactor authentication.
- Follow the steps; a passkey, security key or authenticator app is harder to trick than a text code, but any MFA beats none.
- Save the backup codes somewhere safe and offline.
- Open your phone's or computer's settings and turn on automatic updates.
Words to know:
- Multifactor authentication (MFA): a second proof, after your password, that it is really you.
- Authenticator app: an app that shows sign-in codes that change every few seconds.
- Passkey: a sign-in method that uses your device and face, fingerprint or PIN instead of a password.
- Update / patch: a fix from the maker that closes security holes.
Official sources:
- CISA: Secure Our World
- CISA: More than a password (MFA)
Try it now: Turn on MFA for your email account and save your backup codes. Then check your phone or computer for updates and install any that are waiting.
You can now turn on MFA and keep your devices updated.

check.q: Which of these is an example of a second factor for MFA?
options: Your username
Your favorite color
Your email address
A code from an authenticator app
check.why: MFA asks for a second proof after your password, such as an authenticator code.

check.q: Your phone asks to install an update and restart. What would you do?
options: Ignore it for months
Turn off updates so it stops asking
Install it and restart when asked
Only update if a friend says to
check.why: Updates fix security holes that attackers already know about.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: When something goes wrong
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Follow a simple plan if an account is hacked or a device is infected.
This lesson builds toward: Given signs that an account is hacked or a device is infected, you will write and follow a step-by-step recovery plan, with every key step in a safe order: change the password, turn on MFA, sign out other sessions, check recovery details, warn contacts and report.
Signs of trouble: you cannot sign in, friends get strange messages from you, you see logins or purchases you did not make, or your device suddenly shows pop-ups or runs very slowly.
If an account is hacked: from a safe device, change the password, turn on MFA, sign out of all other sessions (most accounts have this in security settings), and check recovery email and phone numbers. Tell your contacts not to click messages from you. If money is involved, call your bank using the number on your card.
If you clicked a bad link or think a device is infected, the FTC says to update your security software, run a scan and remove anything it flags. At school or work, tell IT right away; reporting fast is not getting in trouble, it limits the damage. Report fraud to ReportFraud.ftc.gov or the FBI's ic3.gov.
Step by step:
- Use a safe device.
- Change the password and turn on MFA.
- Sign out of all other sessions.
- Check recovery email and phone.
- Warn contacts; call your bank if money is involved.
- Update security software and run a scan.
- Tell IT at school or work; report fraud to ReportFraud.ftc.gov or ic3.gov.
Words to know:
- Incident: a security problem, like a hacked account or infected device.
- Session: a place where you are signed in, like a phone or a browser.
- Recovery info: the email and phone a service uses to help you get back into your account.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to recognize and avoid phishing scams
- FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
- FTC: ReportFraud
Try it now: Final task: do a security checkup on your email (strong password in a manager, MFA on, device updated), write your five-line hacked-account plan, and list the phishing signs in one suspicious message.
You can now secure an account end to end and respond calmly if it is ever hacked.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Strong, unique password The password is short, reused or not saved anywhere safe. A password of at least 16 characters, used only on this account, saved in a password manager. Also checks one more important account and makes its password unique. Multifactor authentication MFA is not turned on. MFA is on and working for the account. Uses an authenticator app, passkey or security key instead of a text code. Device up to date Updates were not checked, or automatic updates are off. The phone or computer is up to date and automatic updates are on. Also checks the browser and main apps. Recovery plan The plan is missing or has fewer than three correct steps. Five lines that cover changing the password, MFA, signing out other sessions, checking recovery details and warning contacts. Also says where to report and who to call if money is involved. Phishing signs No message found, or no correct signs listed. One suspicious message with at least two correct phishing signs listed. Also says how and where to report it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which of these is a sign an account may be hacked?
options: Friends get strange messages from you that you did not send
You signed in yesterday
Your password is long
You turned on MFA
check.why: Strange messages sent from your account are a common sign of a takeover.

check.q: At work you think you clicked a bad link. What would you do?
options: Keep quiet so you do not get in trouble
Tell IT right away
Click the link again to check
Turn off MFA
check.why: Reporting fast limits the damage and is not getting in trouble.
